Ahí está la clave, y explica por qué est: There is the key, and it explains why this is really serious. In two dimensions the gradient hardly beats chance (×1.22) because there are few directions in which to go wrong. With 64 dimensions it wins seven times over, and with the hundreds of thousands of numbers of an image the difference is astronomical: a change spread over all the pixels, imperceptible to a person in each pixel separately, is enough to change the answer. It is not that the model sees badly: it is that the space it lives in has very many more directions than our intuition handles.

El primer límite lo señaló <strong>Ada L: The first limit was pointed out by Ada Lovelace in 1843, a hundred years before a computer existed. In her notes to Babbage's analytical engine —notes that are longer than the article she was translating, and that contain the first algorithm published for a machine— she wrote that the machine has no pretension whatever to originate anything: it can do whatever we know how to order it to do. It is the most quoted objection in the history of computing, and Alan Turing argued about it a century later. It is still a good starting point, with one nuance Lovelace could not foresee: today we know how to order it to learn from examples, so that the result can surprise whoever programmed it. What has not changed is where everything it produces comes from: from the data and from the objective somebody chose.
El primer límite ya tiene nombre en este: The first limit already has a name in this course: it is [[cib-segundo-orden|Goodhart's law]], which came up there as a second-order effect of the very act of measuring. It is worth bringing it here because in a system that learns it stops being a management regularity and becomes the exact mechanism by which a model gets worse while its score rises.
El segundo límite se enuncia mal casi si: The second limit is almost always stated badly. It is not that models “have prejudices”, or that their ideology has to be corrected: it is that they learn the data's statistical structure, including the part nobody wanted.
El sesgo no es una opinión del modelo: e: Bias is not the model's opinion: it is the data's statistical structure, including the part nobody wanted. And it does not distinguish correlation from cause because that distinction is not in the data.
El sobreajuste es memorizar ejemplos y f: Overfitting is memorising examples and failing on new ones. Here the model generalises splendidly… to raising the wrong measure.
El tercer límite es el más concreto de l: The third limit is the most concrete of the three, and it comes straight out of [[ia-retropropagacion|backpropagation]]. Esto es [[cib-segundo-orden|un efecto de: This is a textbook [[cib-segundo-orden|second-order effect]]: the intervention changes the system measured. And it appears as soon as a model is fine-tuned by preferences, as you saw in [[ia-llm|the LLM topic]]: if the score rewards answers that look complete, the model learns to produce that appearance, which is cheaper than being correct. No ill intent is needed anywhere.
Estos tres límites deciden cuándo convie: These three limits decide when it is worth using one of these systems and when it is not. Goodhart's law warns that automating a decision changes the behaviour of whoever is evaluated: as soon as it is known what the model looks at, people optimise for it. Inherited bias makes it necessary to measure by groups and not by average, and to demand that that breakdown be published. And adversarial examples argue against these models, as they are, wherever somebody has an interest in fooling them: access control, fraud detection, moderation. In those cases there is a real adversary, and the attack costs one backward pass.
